slides: Okay, a quick summary before the practice.
Everything important about work and rate, in about three minutes.
There's one formula. They give you two of the three, and you find the third.
A rate is always "per". Per minute, per hour. And work is everything you did.
Per hour and per minute in the same question? Convert first.
Same job, twice as fast? Half the time.
Two changes at once? Multiply them. Never add them.
Turn the percent into a fraction. Flip it. And multiply the time.
So twenty-five percent slower does not mean twenty-five percent more time.
No job size? Call the whole job one.
Or pick a job size. Four hours and ten hours? A job of twenty units. So that's five and two units per hour. No fractions.
Working together? Add the rates. Never add the completion times.
A drain, or a leak, gets a minus.
A nice common time? Stretch both workers to it, and then add.
Times over plus... that's for exactly two workers. And two equal workers? Half the time.
Three hours and six hours? The answer is between one and a half and three. So cross out everything outside that first.
Identical workers, and a group? That's a team question. Work always sits in the middle.
Put the question row second. Blank in Team or Time? Use the V. Blank in Work? The V upside down.
Then a quick sense check of the direction.
Worker-hours measure the size of the job. One worker alone needs that many hours.
Someone joins, or leaves? The whole job, minus what's done, is what's left.
It's not the average of the rates. More time goes to the slow rate, so the answer is closer to it.
So, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: adding times instead of rates, taking a percent in the rate as the same percent in the time, averaging two rates, and mixing minutes with hours.
Good luck.
